name: Andi Toma
editorial_article:
Andi Toma is a German electronic musician and producer, widely celebrated as one half of the influential experimental electronic duo Mouse on Mars. Born and raised in Germany, Toma, alongside his longtime collaborator Jan St. Werner, established Mouse on Mars in 1993, rapidly becoming one of the most inventive forces in the international electronic music scene. Their work is characterized by a restless, anarchic, and intellectually rigorous approach to sound design, purposefully straddling the lines between pop music, avant-garde experimentation, art, and club culture. Rejecting conventional genre constraints, Toma’s production style is marked by a complex interplay of chaotic noise, meticulous sonic layering, and a playful, often humorous, approach to musical structure.

Throughout their multi-decade career, Toma and St. Werner have consistently refused to settle into a static aesthetic, instead pursuing a "dialectical method" of production where they continuously decompose and reconstruct their sound. This has resulted in a vast and multifaceted discography that explores everything from IDM and techno to ambient and orchestral compositions. Beyond their output as Mouse on Mars, Toma has been an integral figure in the German music scene, co-founding the highly respected independent label Sonig, which serves as a platform for experimental and genre-defying artists. His collaborative spirit extends well beyond the electronic medium, including notable projects with figures like Stereolab’s Laetitia Sadier (as part of the collective musical ecosystem), and his involvement in experimental projects like Microstoria (with Markus Popp) and Von Südenfed (with Mark E. Smith).

Toma’s influence is grounded in his willingness to embrace unpredictability and his commitment to cross-disciplinary exchange. Whether performing live with traditional instruments alongside complex programmed electronic interfaces or developing bespoke music software like the fluXpad app, he consistently bridges the divide between the intellectual rigor of academic research and the visceral, sensory experience of the dancefloor. His work remains a defining example of the experimental potential of electronic music, continuing to push the boundaries of what is possible within the medium.
